tagline.text: A mangrove eco-park in Ibajay with 27 species and a 1.7 km boardwalk

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangays Bugtongbato and Naisud, Ibajay, Aklan, about 34 km west of Kalibo

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~700 (per person, entrance fee, transport and meals, as a day trip from Kalibo)

children.text: Katunggan It Ibajay Eco-Park is a 44-hectare mangrove forest on the tidal flats of Ibajay in western Aklan. Twenty-seven of the Philippines' 30 mangrove species grow here, and the timber boardwalk extended in 2021 now totals about 1.7 km.

Katunggan It Ibajay Eco-Park is a mangrove eco-park spanning Barangays Bugtongbato and Naisud in the municipality of Ibajay, Aklan. In the local language, "katunggan" means a mangrove forest. In August 2025 the local newspaper Daily Guardian gave its area as 44.22 hectares and reported that it was established by Municipal Ordinance No. 092 in 2009. The official opening took place on January 19, 2010. Ibajay lies about 34 km west of Kalibo, and Wikipedia says the drive takes 45 minutes to 1 hour. It sits on the western Aklan road between Kalibo and Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay, so it is a handy stop on the way to or from Boracay. Ibajay is made up of 35 barangays, covers about 158.9 square kilometers and had about 53,000 people in the 2024 census. Wikipedia calls it the "Heart of Western Aklan."

What makes this place special is its variety of species. Daily Guardian says 27 of the Philippines' 30 mangrove species grow in the park (Wikipedia says 28 and the 2010 opening speech says 27, so sources differ by one species). The forest is dominated by Avicennia trees, known locally as apiapi or bungalon, and a stand of centuries-old Avicennia rumphiana is nicknamed the "avatar tree." There is also a nursery for gapas-gapas (Camptostemon philippinense), which the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) considers endangered. Birds, mangrove lobsters, fiddler crabs and mudskippers live here, so it also works as a place to watch nature.

Local residents did much to keep the forest as it is. According to the opening speech by a SEAFDEC researcher, when researchers visited in the late 1990s there were moves to cut trees to make fishponds, and in the 1980s residents and officials used "People Power" to stop chainsaws. In 2008, support came from the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), and a small grant from the Pew foundation in 2005 paid for the first stretch of walkway. Today the park is managed by the Ibajay municipal government, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and ZSL, and the Bugtongbato Fisherfolk Association and the Naisud Mangrove and Aquatic Organizations take part in running it on site. Entrance income goes toward maintaining park facilities and community livelihood projects.

The facilities center on the timber boardwalk. In September 2021, with support from Senator Loren Legarda, a 1.6 km section was added, bringing the total boardwalk to about 1.747 km. There is also a 132-square-meter viewing deck and signs that explain how mangroves help ease climate change. Newspapers of the same period reported a 400-meter section opening separately, so section lengths differ by source. Check the actual length on site before you go. Besides walking, visitors can look at old trees, plant mangroves, kayak and fish.
The center of the park is a walkway stretching over the mangrove forest. After the September 2021 extension it is said to total about
, and the handrails make it easy to walk. The length varies by source, so confirm it locally.

Along the boardwalk there are viewing spots overlooking the mangroves and the mudflats, and the largest deck covers 132 square meters. The light is soft in the early morning or late afternoon, which is good for photos.
This is where the centuries-old Avicennia rumphiana (bungalon) grow. According to the opening speech, it was about
10 minutes
on foot from the ceremony site. Check with a local guide whether it is still in the same place.

Twenty-seven of the Philippines' 30 mangrove species are said to grow here. Leaves and roots differ from species to species, so walking while listening to the signs and a local guide makes it far more interesting.

The park runs a mangrove nursery focused on gapas-gapas, a species the IUCN considers endangered. It is an effort to raise species diversity, and whether visitors can look at the seedlings should be confirmed locally.
The park is described as offering kayaking and fishing experiences. Equipment and fees are explained by the local operating groups, and operations change with the tide.
Birds and mudflat animals such as mangrove lobsters, fiddler crabs and mudskippers live here. At low tide, if you look over the mud you can see crabs and mudskippers moving, so walk quietly.

blocks.title: A park the village tends together

children.text: Community groups from Bugtongbato and Naisud take part in running the park. Entrance fees and souvenir purchases go toward village livelihoods and upkeep, so listening to your guide and spending even a little at local shops helps.
Take a bus, van or jeepney from Kalibo toward Ibajay. Ibajay is about
34 km
from Kalibo.
Get off in downtown Ibajay and take a tricycle to the park entrance in Bugtongbato.
Pay the entrance fee at the entrance and start walking the boardwalk with a guide.
Look around the viewing deck and the old Avicennia stand.
Ask whether kayaking or fishing is available, and enjoy a short session if it is.
Return to downtown Ibajay for lunch, then move on to Kalibo or Caticlan.
There is little shade on the boardwalk, so early morning is recommended. Rides back may be infrequent, so check the last departure in advance.
Walk the boardwalk at Katunggan It Ibajay Eco-Park.
Have lunch in downtown Ibajay.
Choose either Ibajay Beach or Sniba-a Falls in the village of Aparicio (a short mountain trail). Go with a local guide to the falls.
Head back to Kalibo or Caticlan.
The trail to the falls is slippery in the rainy season, so the beach is the safer choice. Ask the municipal office about current access.
Direct flights run from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Kalibo International Airport (KLO) in about
1 hour
. Check airlines and schedules when you book.
From KLO, you reach Ibajay by road, passing through Kalibo and heading west.
From Kalibo to Ibajay it is about
34 km
by road, and Wikipedia says it takes
45 minutes to 1 hour
. You can find buses, vans and jeepneys to Ibajay at Kalibo's terminals. Check fares and operating hours locally.
Ibajay lies on the western route linking Kalibo with Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay, so you can also take a vehicle heading for Boracay and get off at Ibajay.
From downtown Ibajay, take a tricycle to the park entrance. Search results note that a special fare may apply for the ride from town, so agree on the price before you ride.
Some sources give the park's hours as 7 AM to 5 PM, but they can change, so check with the tourism office or the park before you visit.

The boardwalk is slippery in the rain, and in the wet season the mudflats and paths get muddy. The dry season from November to May is best for walking, and with little shade at midday, an early start is recommended.

January is the time of Kalibo's Ati-Atihan, and Ibajay also holds its own big Ati-Atihan on the fourth Sunday of January. On festival days the roads are crowded and lodging runs short, so book early to match your plans. The dates change each year, so check the latest announcements.

rows: Best for walking, and the Ibajay Ati-Atihan festival is in January
Go early morning or late afternoon, hat and water essential
The boardwalk is slippery and showers are frequent, so bring a raincoat and sandals

There are no large lodgings around the park, so most people stay in Kalibo or on Boracay and come for the day. Downtown Ibajay may have small guesthouses, but the choice is not wide, so check the latest reviews on a booking site. During the January Ati-Atihan festival, lodging fills up early, so reserve ahead.

The easiest way to eat is at restaurants or the market in downtown Ibajay. Local seafood is common, but the menu and hours of any restaurant in the park were not confirmed, so bring water and snacks. There may be no shop along the walk, so buy bottled water at the entrance. Many places want cash, so carry small bills.
Early morning is best for spotting birds and avoiding the midday heat.
There is little shade on the boardwalk, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Ask a guide about the location of the old trees and the nursery for the most accurate answer.
It is handy to ask a tricycle driver to wait for your return, but agree on the price first.
Low tide is good for seeing mudflat life, and high tide is better for kayaking. Ask your guide about the tide.
Entrance fees and hours differ by source, so check with the park or the municipal office before you go.
Wear sandals or sneakers that do not slip.
Mangroves are protected, so do not break branches or leave trash.

Ibajay is also known for its Ati-Atihan on the fourth Sunday of January, so if you go in January, plan to combine the park and the festival in one day. Roads jam on festival days, so see the park first and head into town in the afternoon.
Right after rain the boardwalk floor and handrails are wet and slippery, so slow your pace and keep your camera and phone in a waterproof pouch.
Boardwalk length (from about 400 m to 1.7 km) and the entrance fee differ by news report and blog. This text covers what could be confirmed, so follow the latest local guidance.
The boardwalk is slippery in the rain and some sections may be damaged, so hold the handrail as you walk.
Public transport to the park is limited and it can be hard to catch a ride back, so check the last departure in advance.
Kayaking and fishing may not be possible depending on the tide and the operating groups.
The boardwalk gets dark after sunset, so leave early in the afternoon.
The forest and mudflats are protected, so do not touch or take any plants or animals.
About
34 km
to the east, the Aklan capital
Kalibo
has a cathedral, a museum and a market.
The
Ati-Atihan Festival
, held in Kalibo every January, pairs well with Ibajay's festival.
Reached via Caticlan,
Boracay
is the famous beach destination that lies beyond Ibajay.

Ibajay Beach runs along the coast across 10 barangays, and Sniba-a Falls in Aparicio is reached by a short mountain trail. Nawidwid Falls and Su-ag Falls in Mina-a village are also there, so you can keep going with nature sights.
